blocks.x: The Homer Bond.
Homer Bond and Tiger Rag.
If you have Tiger Rag on, it should be easy to find because people bought Tiger Rag.
Tiger Rag on the one side and the Homer Bond on the other.
Yeah, and this is Paramount and then what year?
I think it's around 22, I'd say 22 or 23.

Well, it was very early in the first period of Paramount. Inc. must have started with them right at the outset, didn't it? They had ink started with them just as soon as they started recording stuff on the south side. Yeah, yeah. Inc. must have been there very early. Well, I'll see what I can find. Where are your notes, Jasper? I'd like to go over those with the films. Who is on the record? Did you give Jasper that information? Oh, yeah. He has that. Ernest Tapley, huh? Banjo? Banjo. Where'd he come from?
He stayed on the south side, right at 28th and LaSalle at the time.
Did these fellas all come from Louisville with you?
No, no, neither. He lived with his father.
You don't know where Tapley came from originally?
No, I do not.
James Turner?
He lived here already. He was an original Louisville Jug Band. Mm-hmm. That, they're the names you don't can't remember the banjo. Mm-hmm.

Well, this is the group that made the Paramount, anyway, and you used a nose whistle on that. Yeah. And it was called Jones So Different Four. So Different Four. Uh, Sal Turner was a guitar, and you had the nose whistle. That's right. And there was the four of you on it. Four of us. Um, did you make other titles than this?
No, I never made but one record.
This is your record, okay.
It's the most record I ever made. Uh-huh.

Do you ever hear a nose whistle? No. Play it for him a little bit, and we'll see how it records, and then I'll play it back on then. Gee, I appreciate that. I asked him to bring it because I wanted to put a little on the tape just to have the tonality of it, because I hear a lot of instruments, I don't know what they are.
stuff Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.
I used to play it, but I can't play it now. It takes so much will.

Well, Mr. Harvey Jones, let's go back. Jasper Taylor, I'll play it back in a minute, but as long as it's still running, I thought we'd pick up some of this stuff. Now, Jasper said you were born where? Versailles, Kentucky. They call it Versailles in France and they call it Versailles in Kentucky, huh?
Well, it's Versailles, Kentucky.
Yeah. Uh, January 27, 1902. Is that right?
That's right.
And your mother, is this?
Oh, that's my wife.
Oh, your wife, Sinobie.
Sinobie is here.
What was your mother's name?
Charlotte.
How's it spelled?
Charlotte. C-H-L-I-O-T-T-E.
Oh, yes. And your father?
Uh, uh, Henry Jones.
Henry. Uh, and you went to college, did you?
I had my wife.
Oh, that, your wife went to college. All right. And she too was born in Versailles.
Right.
Uh, it was Simmons University that she went to. That's right. Um, now is this, uh, uh, your present wife?
Yeah, that's my present wife.
Well, you were married previously though, huh? No. No? Gee, you stayed a bachelor a long time. Forty, forty-four years. Yeah, I married. Wow, good for you. I was six.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Um, now about 1920 is this? You were about 18, you joined the Louisville Jug Band?
Right. Uh... I came to Chicago in 1920 with the Louisville Jug Band.
Oh, with them. All right. And then you'd been rehearsing a little bit with them and had something worked out and you brought it into Chicago to sell it.
No, they saw me working around in Louisville and they picked me up and asked me if I wanted a job with them.
Oh, was this the Nose Whistle act that you were doing that they wanted?

Oh, yeah. I danced and sing all around the whole, tabbing and things. I was just, uh, one of them little boys jumping up around the street, singing and dancing, and they, they liked what I was doing. Figured I would be a great novelty with the band, so they had taken me on.
How big a group was the band when you joined them?
They had three outside of them, I said it was four. Uh-huh. Four of them.
Well, and Jasper's written down the names of some of them here. Louie Leslie, guitar. Yeah, guitar. And Earl McDonald, Jug. And it was his band. It was his band.
And he was a leader.
And you had a banjo and you didn't remember...
I can't think of the boy's name.
And a banjo.
I've forgotten his name.
There were several jugs around Louisville. Now, was McDonald a pretty prominent one?
McDonald was the original.

He was the first one around those all. He was the original Jug Blower. Did you ever encounter, Jasper, did you ever encounter jug bands before 20? Well, yes, I saw the original across the street from the barbershop. I played over there. Well, was it this group or another? It was this group. Not Grandy. Yeah. I knew Grandy. He played. All right. Grandy came later. He also played jug. But I wondered if there were other jug bands before this thing started in Louisville. Now, in Louisville there were several jugs blowing after a while. But had you heard of any in 1915 or 16 or anywhere? The Louisville Jug Band was my first one. First encounter. I haven't heard of a jug down in New Orleans, but I wonder if it could have started around Louisville that's effect out of a jug. Do you play that?

That's the only one that I know of is Earl McDonnell. I know several that come up after he did, but I never did pay any attention to them, because they weren't the rich one, and they didn't get no jobs in the first beginning. They never was put out or hired for no fine jobs and things like that. But Earl, he showed the Hippodrome, New York, and all the biggest, finest places you could find. He wasn't hired. And when we came here to Chicago in 20, we was hired by Jack Rees. Jack Rees had a cabaret at Ohio on State Street, classic cabaret.

Classic cabaret. I'll have to, frequently in all telephone books I can find out the exact location, the telephone number. and address. But Ohio on State. That's where it was. On the corner? It's about the second door from the corner. Which corner, do you remember? Going east. North or south? East.
Going east. Going towards the lake.
Going east on the south side or north side of the street?
It was on the east side of the street. It was on the north side going...
North, northeast corner.
Near the northeast corner. North, northeast corner.
Jack Rees, classic cabaret. Yeah, yeah. And is this where they had a, they also had a white band?
Yeah, Purple Derbies.
Or was this another place?
That's the same place, Purple Derbies.
Purple Derbies was the name of the band? That was the name of the band.
Uh-huh.
I can...
It was a white band.
Yeah. You don't remember anybody in that band?
I can't remember those fellas. They saved my life.
Did Jack Reed bring you up from Louisville or did you come on the chance that you'd pick
up a cab? No, he brought us a cab. Brought you up. We had a contract for that job.
Did McDonald go on the road before this time? Had he been on the road?
Yeah, he'd been to New York, played the Hippodrome Theater, several games in New York for Charles Dillian Yes, I remember that name.
Yeah, he was. How long had McDonald been in the music business before 1920?
Oh, I guess he'd been in the music business eight or nine years before I ever met him. He played around that road for years with the Ballast Flower Company. Ballast Flower.
Now, the Flower Company had some radio programs, too. Is that where you...
That's the same. He was on that program.
Well, that started after 1920, I think. Now, did he work too far before?
He started before then. Is that so? Yeah, he was working there when I joined him, when he got this and gave him to come to Chicago in 1920.
Do you remember that McDonald did other recording, did recording work?
No, I do not know.
There are some records in the name of Louisville Jug Band, but I think that's Clifford Hayes' group.
I don't know. I wouldn't say because I don't know, but I do know he made a record, made some records. I don't know. They were famous when I started working with them. They were famous.
After they worked the Classic Cabaret for about eleven months, do you remember where you went then?
Where I went?
Oh, yeah. Were you, did you stay with the band?

No, the band left me here. Oh. The band left me, went on back to Louisville. I stayed here and made records with the Power Mount Company, and I had a band of my own, a little four piece and five piece, combo band. I played all around in the various night club, Kelly's Stable, Sherman House.

You played Sherman? Yeah, I played Sherman House. Yeah. All right. Then with that, with that group you made the Paramount record. Now that was your first group in about 1922, and Homer Brown Blues on Paramount and Tiger Rag on the reverse. This is the one with Ernest Tapley, Banjo, James Turner, guitar, Saul Turner. Was he a brother?
No, he was just a friend of ours.
Well, I mean the two Turners. I mean the two Turners.
No, no relation.
Guitar and Harvey Jones. And then you had a second group. How much later was that?
That was about a year later.
You had a fellow named Heebie-Jeebies?
Heebie-Jeebies and Elijah Cross.
What was Cross's name?
Elijah.
Elijah Cross. And you still had Sol Turner.
Sol Turner and Heebie-Jeebies.
I suppose you did vocals too?
Oh, yeah. Actually, all four of us, three of us sang together. And what mostly I did was play this horn and my other horn, and sang and danced.
You mentioned Tick Young's Cabaret.
That's at 95th and Western.
I was unfamiliar with that place. Did you stay there a while?
Oh, I stayed at Tick Young's, I guess. Enough to stay in jail all the time. Back and forth with the gangsters. Yeah, I stayed there about five, six months after Tick Young's.
And you do trumpet effects on the nose whistle, and so they called you the second Louis Armstrong, yeah?
That was when I was playing that other horn, but not on the other horn.
Oh, on the other horn. Yeah. Now, what is the other horn?

The other horn was a jazz sax. It was made like a, the bella was made like a trumpet. The bella was made like a trumpet, and it had a little end that'd come out for mouthpiece, and had another end that'd go down like that, where your water and stuff would come out. And you'd play that just like you'd play a trumpet. And I, at that time, I, I had a timid voice, and I could play high and make it sound just like a trumpet. So I played that in several bands when I was playing in nightclubs around here. I can't think of a fella on the club.
Well, how'd you get the tone? Was it an effect like a kazoo?

Yeah, it's the same effect like a kazoo, but only I had a, a tone that none of the rest fellas couldn't get. Of course, I could play high and I'd play so true. You didn't sound like a kazoo. If you could have a, if you run into this record I was telling you about, you, you couldn't detect it from the trumpet.
You use that on the, uh, Homeward Brown?
Homeward Brown Blues and the Tiger Rag.
Yeah. I sure will look for it because that'd be interesting. You couldn't, you couldn't hardly detect it. And, uh, and the nose whistle, though, was more a clarinet type.
That's more clarinet effect.
Well, now, is, is this the instrument that's called a human tone? This is it. That's right. Human tone. There we go. That's the name of it. It's right on there.
Yeah. Yeah. Sure enough. Have you almost same time?
Yes, something like that. You use your voice to shape the, the...

You can't, you can't play that with no voice. No? You've got to blow that through your nose. You can't play that no kind of way in the world unless you blow through your nose. Oh, you are, you are whistling through your nose. That's right. You're blowing through.
Are you recording?
Am I interrupting? No. No,
There's no problem at all. But I, I caught it with my mouth. Now you can see how you, how you, see how you do that?
Yeah. Shhh, shhh, shhh.
And you drop your bottom lip here. Oh.
See. That's right. That's right. The mouth is a, is a sound box. That's right. Yeah. Resonating chamber.

You can't play that. You can't. You can do, holler anything you want through here. You can't play nothing. Yeah. But you've got to play that for your nose. And you caught it. You have to call it. You changed the tone with the change. Yeah. That's the only way. Now I used to be good with this, but I, I haven't played this since 40.
Well, it sounds, it sounds to me as if it wouldn't take you long to be very good.

Well, I, since I had my teeth drawn, you know, I had my teeth and take my bare teeth take out and have some force put in where it's pretty hard to control it. Because you mostly have to control it with your tongue and the low end of your mouth, see. And this bridge won't let me get my tongue as fast as I used to play this here.
It tells me how he ran into tooth trouble. He used to do some acts where he'd balance chairs and tables in his mouth.
Okay. See, I stayed in show business 25 years. I traveled all over the country, that's for sure.
Mainly with these musical acts or dancing?
I played in white night club, played in white theaters, played in the finest places you could find from the show boat in St. Louis on down. Played all over the country.
You play any of the Chicago clubs besides those that you mentioned?
No, I played all these night clubs, but in them days they called them gangsters places. I remember gangsters ran those places. And I played in all them joints.
Dreamland or entertainers? Dreamland was 35th State? Yeah.

No, I never played there. I never played in no colored night club at all. All white. That's right. Over on Lake Street, 63rd and Nairobi, 95th and Western, on Ray Street, so many different night clubs, I couldn't call the name of them.
The white places pay a little better?
Sure, I made $150, $200 a night. Who's that for? I made it as high as $100 a night at the Classic Cabaret. Never touched my salary. That was a worth of thought.
Well, maybe it's worth losing your teeth.
Well, at that time I wasn't dancing right up in here. See, I was on the road. I did Aquabat for a while on the road. Do much theater work?
Oh, yeah.

On the TOBA time, we called it then, we played all Chattanooga, Atlanta, Georgia, Memphis, New Orleans, Jackson, Mississippi, Birmingham, Mobile, Alabama, all around through that part of country. When was that about?
What part of your career?

Oh, that was in the, I was in, from 40 on, from 1940, during the 40. But from 1928 until 1940, I was with the Vaudeville show then. I stayed on one show nine years down in Texas. P.J. Tidwell's Carnival. I stayed there. I was a leading comedian down there for nine years. And then when I came off of that, then I came back and joined the Brown Skin Models out of New York.
Oh, yes, I remember that.
I closed with them in St. Dusty, Ohio in 41.
Well, it wasn't called TOBA after 40, was it? Or is the TOBA?
There wasn't no TOBA in 40.
No, when was the TOBA period?
Back there from, from, well, I say when I ran into it, it was in 28, but there had been TOBA before then.
Yeah, yeah, yeah, that must have, TOBA must have started by the middle 20s sometime, 24 or 25.
Way back there.
You play any Chicago theaters? Haymarket.
Oh, yeah. Played Haymarket Theater. That's the only theater I play in.
Well, that's, that's a very interesting career. Here's something about you playing drums with Sam Clark's band in Versace.
I was at home then, I was in my team. I was a young boy, playing drums. He had all four of them learned how to play drums.
That'd be maybe around the war years, huh?

Yeah, yeah. First of all, Mark? See, I was a young fella, young man. I was playing Sam Clark, I was a young man. How'd you spend in show business? No, I retired from show business in 1940 when I came back there, came back there in 45, but I retired from show business in 42. And I come back scrubbing in 45. In 1945? Mm-hmm. Yeah, I left there in 27, and I didn't come back here when I moved in 45.
Yeah, Versace is in Woodward County, isn't it?
Woodford County.
Woodford. Uh, yeah, it's, it's spelled the same as Versace. Woodford County. Um, do you remember anybody in Sam Clark's band?
Yeah, there's, uh, Fessal Mack. He was a trumpet player. George Brown.
Was that the fella they called Red Mack later? Or Shorty Mack?
I don't know what Shorty Mack was. We called him Fess. Fess Mack.
Fess Mack.

He was a trumpet player. Another boy named George Brown, he was a trumpet player. And we had a fella play with us during that time called Jack Molasses. Now he was a guitar player. Another fella played the violin, in those days they called them fiddles. His name was Claire Wilson. And I played drums then with them.
And what was Clark's instrument?
He was, he was a drummer.
He played drums. But you, you played drums too with the band.

Well, I learned, he liked me drums. I see. You see. Well, he, I learned drums on him when I was in school. I put drumming down. I bought a set of drums from Werlitz out of Cincinnati. I think I gave eighty dollars for a set of drums. And I kept them drums. I don't know what ever happened to them drumming, because I got tired of food when I put them down. And I left home with the...
How'd you get on to the feeling that you wanted to go into the theatrical business? Anything happen?

Well, I'll tell you, I'll tell you about that not too long story. You know, in Kentucky you have a lot of hard work, such as farming, and tobacco, and wheat, and corn, and hemp. Well, I wasn't cut out from the whole lot of hard work, you know, because he wasn't paying nothing.
Well, the size of you too. You'd cut out from the...

Yeah, I was a pretty young fellow. And I didn't care for that hard work, and the whole rest of my brothers, and my father, they worked hard, and things. But I said I wasn't going to never let no hard work kill me. So I used to dance so much all around the streets, so there were all the white people in my home, thought there wasn't nobody there to beat me dancing. And the show came through there, or Carnival, came through there. Johnny J. Jones was Carnival. Sure. And they had a fellow on there named Friday. And they was putting out chances, and a little money behind it, if anybody could beat Friday dancing, you know.
You were challenging, isn't it?

Yeah, so they put me up on Friday. Yeah. And I beat Friday. At least the hometown went for me, you know. And I beat him dancing. And so that made me think then that I was a great dancer, North Van Al-Smoke-Sale. So I said, well, if I'm that great, I'm going to leave him. So I did. I left home with W.M. Morris Carnival.
Well, you aren't so different, I think, from the rest of us, Mr. Jones. We figure out what's easiest for us to do with it. We don't like hard work either.

Well, I found it paid off. And, but I put drumming down because it looked like I had no trouble going to theaters. Everybody beat me to the theater, and I'd be back at Luggan with all them drums and things. And I said I'd let the drums go, and I'd taken up comedy.

Well, you were very good in deciding on some of these novelty instruments, because there's a fine feel for it if you can concentrate on it enough to learn to do it properly. I think Jasper saw that too. He came up with novelty ideas, you know, that made quite a name for him. Yeah. Without those novelty instruments, a lot of people would just know you as a drummer, and that's all, huh? Yeah.
Well, I enjoyed all my choker, and, yeah.
Uh, uh, uh, it would take nothing for it. Just, uh, yeah.
But what I learned, and I learned more than that. Mm-hmm. And choker didn't ever learn anything else.
All right. Oh, yes, yes, sir.
You want some? No, I have some.
Can you share it, or? Yeah.
Most I, most I really didn't like was a minstrel show. I was. Did you work with minstrels? Oh, yeah.
Now, you mentioned Rabbit's Foot, didn't you?
Yeah.
When, when were you with Rabbit's Foot?
I was at Radford in 1940.
Well, now, this wasn't the, the old Rabbit's Foot in, that was in the 20s, was it? Did you mind if I was there?
Yeah, but they, but they was operating, uh, with the, uh, they had a railroad show then, but this time, when I was on with them, they had the buses. Yeah.
But it was the same organization. Same organization.
Ma Rainey was with Rabbit's Foot, wasn't she? That was, yes. That way before I went on. I don't know.

That was, that was funny, in the 20s. Pat Shaffell, I saw it when I was a kid. Uh-huh. Walcott and bought the rights. Mm-hmm. Yeah. Pat Shaffell's, Rabbit's Foot. But, uh, you were with the Rabbit's Foot. Anybody that we'd know, uh, with that outfit then, do you know who had the band?

Yeah, I know who had the band. And, uh, Hosey Sapp. I heard that on that. A boy, a boy from, uh, Tampa, Florida. He, uh, he had the band. Hosey Sapp. Hosey Sapp. He had that band when I was in Jarmine. And, uh, uh, and, uh, well, originally Joe White, he was still there. I guess you heard of Joe White, he been there for the, been a rap for the, ever since he was a boy. The whole thing, Mandy Cameroy was with him once. As a drummer.
As a drummer.
As a drummer, street drummer.
Mm-hmm.
But Hosey Sapp had the band when I was on that. And Hosey Sapp has caused me being on, uh, on, uh, uh, Brown Skin Marvel. About stuff

When they were trying to find a comedian, I happened to be in New Orleans at the time at the palace. I stayed there seven weeks at the palace doing a single. And they couldn't find nobody to hold down the spot. But they had a fellow there named Jazz Richardson. He was a mighty great comedian at the time, but somehow, I don't know where they let him go, I think. I don't know where they didn't do something right or something wrong, anyhow, they let him go. I said, well, they came to New Orleans and were looking for a comic, and they're lucky enough to find me there, because I had laid where Rapsford had closed. We closed the show, St. Joe, Mississippi. And I went on to Natchez. I stopped in Natchez. I stayed in Natchez there. Oh, I guess I was in Natchez about a couple of months.
Don't miss New Orleans now. The theater is telling about it. Well, the palace. Before Natchez, you know.

Oh, well, that was at the palace in the Lincoln. Yeah, you were. It was the same man who owned the palace, owned the Lincoln, too. And I showed both theaters there. And I left there and went on over to the...
Today, the comedians often buy an act that's all set up for them. In your day, did you have to work out your own material, or did you work from a script that somebody else would write up?

Sometimes. Sometimes, if a fella had something he wanted you to pull over his way, you tried his way. But as a rule, when I hired a man with his show, I had my own act. Yeah. See, I had my own act. See, I'm a Russian dancer. I do Russian dancing. I do wings. I do rhythm. I do clog. And I sings. My own numbers.
Well, so you'd have your act in the Oleo, and you might be in the...
I'd have my act in...

segments.title: The Paramount record and the So Different Four lineup
segments.summary: Allen and Jones go over the Paramount record of Homeward Bound Blues and Tiger Rag, its date and sidemen (Tapley, the Turners). Jones's nose whistle is played for the tape.

segments.title: Birth in Versailles, Kentucky, parents and wife
segments.summary: Jones gives his birth date and place, his parents' names, and talks about his wife Sinobie, who attended Simmons University, and their long marriage.

segments.title: Joining Earl McDonald's Louisville Jug Band
segments.summary: The band picked Jones up as a dancing and singing novelty at about 18. He names members and says McDonald was the original jug blower and leader.

segments.title: Jug bands before and after McDonald
segments.summary: Allen and Jasper Taylor ask about earlier jug bands. Jones says only McDonald got fine jobs, including the Hippodrome in New York, before coming to Chicago.

segments.title: Jack Rees's Classic Cabaret on State Street
segments.summary: The band was hired under contract by Jack Rees for his cabaret in Chicago. They talk about its location and the white Purple Derbies band.

segments.title: McDonald's earlier career and recordings
segments.summary: Jones recalls McDonald's New York dates, his years on the road with a flower company, and the band's fame, but is unsure about their recordings.

segments.title: Staying in Chicago with his own combos and Paramount records
segments.summary: After about eleven months the band returned to Louisville but Jones stayed, formed small combos, and played Kelly's Stable and the Sherman House. He describes the first and second groups (Turners, Elijah Cross, Heebie-Jeebies).

segments.title: Tick Young's Cabaret and the trumpet-like jazz sax
segments.summary: Jones describes his months at Tick Young's, and the horn he played that sounded like a trumpet, earning him the nickname second Louis Armstrong, versus the clarinet-like nose whistle.

segments.title: How the nose whistle (human tone) is played
segments.summary: Jones demonstrates blowing through the nose and shaping tone with the mouth, and says dental work has ended his playing.

segments.title: Chicago white clubs, gangsters and pay
segments.summary: Jones played white nightclubs and theaters, run by gangsters, never colored clubs. He made $150-200 a night and talks about the Haymarket.

segments.title: TOBA circuit, carnival years and Brown Skin Models
segments.summary: Jones lists TOBA theaters in the South, nine years as comedian with P.J. Tidwell's Carnival from 1928, then the Brown Skin Models until 1941. They discuss when TOBA existed.

segments.title: Playing drums in Sam Clark's band in Versailles
segments.summary: Jones recalls drumming as a young man in Sam Clark's band at home, naming members, and buying a drum set, and when he retired and returned.

segments.title: Beating Friday at dancing and leaving home with a carnival
segments.summary: Jones explains he avoided farm work, beat the carnival dancer Friday, left with the W.M. Morris Carnival and gave up drums for comedy.

segments.title: Rabbit's Foot Minstrels and Brown Skin Models
segments.summary: Jones dislikes minstrel shows, talks about the Rabbit's Foot in 1940, bandleader Hosey Sapp, and how he got the comedian spot in New Orleans theaters.

segments.title: Comedy material and his own act
segments.summary: Jones says he usually did his own act, including Russian dancing, clog and singing his own numbers.
